text: An X-ray is a form of high-energy electromagnetic radiation with a wavelength shorter than ultraviolet rays and longer than gamma rays, ranging from 10 nanometers to 10 picometers, corresponding to frequencies between 30 petahertz and 30 exahertz (3×10¹⁶ Hz to 3×10¹⁹ Hz) and photon energies from 100 eV to 100 keV. Discovered in 1895 by German scientist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, who named it X-radiation to signify its unknown nature, X-rays can penetrate solid substances like construction materials and living tissue, making them valuable in medical diagnostics (e.g., detecting broken bones) and materials science (e.g., identifying chemical elements and detecting flaws in materials). However, as ionizing radiation, X-rays pose health risks such as DNA damage, cancer, burns, and radiation sickness, leading to strict regulatory control. Early observations of X-rays date back to experiments with discharge tubes investigating cathode rays, first observed in 1869; these rays were produced in Crookes tubes (invented around 1875) when high DC voltages (between a few kilovolts and 100 kV) accelerated electrons that struck the anode or glass wall, generating X-rays. William Morgan reported in 1785 on effects from electrical currents in partially evacuated glass tubes, later explored by Humphry Davy and Michael Faraday. In 1888, Philipp Lenard found that cathode rays could pass through a thin aluminum window in a Crookes tube, exposing photographic plates and causing fluorescence; some of these "Lenard rays" were likely X-rays. Hermann von Helmholtz developed mathematical equations and a dispersion theory for X-rays based on electromagnetic theory before Röntgen’s discovery but did not work with actual X-rays. In early 1890, William Jennings and Arthur W. Goodspeed accidentally produced an X-ray image while photographing coins with electric sparks, though they did not claim a discovery. Ludwig Zehnder, Röntgen’s assistant, noticed a flash of light from a fluorescent screen before a covered tube was switched on. In 1891–1893, Fernando Sanford also likely produced and detected X-rays during "electric photography" experiments. Nikola Tesla noticed damaged film linked to Crookes tubes and began investigating invisible radiant energy; after Röntgen’s discovery, Tesla used high voltages and custom tubes to produce X-ray images. On 8 November 1895, Röntgen discovered X-rays while experimenting with Lenard and Crookes tubes, writing a preliminary report titled "On a new kind of ray" and submitting it to the Würzburg Physical-Medical Society on 28 December 1895. He referred to the radiation as "X" to indicate its unknown nature, with some early texts calling it Chi-rays. Due to the loss of Röntgen’s lab notes after his death, the discovery account is reconstructed: he was testing cathode rays in a Crookes tube wrapped in black cardboard, using a barium platinocyanide screen, when he observed a faint green glow 1 meter away, realizing invisible rays were passing through the cardboard and through books and paper. He systematically studied these rays and published his findings two months later. Röntgen discovered their medical use when he took a photograph of his wife’s hand, the first human body part image using X-rays; she reportedly said, "I have seen my death." The discovery sparked widespread interest, with Otto Glasser estimating 49 essays and 1044 articles published in 1896 alone, and Science dedicating 23 articles to it that year. Sensationalist reactions included links to telepathy and occult theories. The name X-rays persisted despite colleagues suggesting "Röntgen rays," which are still used in many languages. Röntgen received the inaugural Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery. He immediately recognized medical applications and sent letters to physicians in Europe in January 1896. Alan Archibald Campbell-Swinton was the first to create an X-ray photograph (of a hand) after Röntgen, and by February 1896, 46 experimenters in North America were using the technique. The first clinical use was by John Hall-Edwards in Birmingham, England on 11 January 1896, when he radiographed a needle in an associate’s hand, and on 14 February 1896, he performed the first surgical use of X-rays. In early 1896, Ivan Romanovich Tarkhanov irradiated frogs and insects, concluding X-rays affected living functions. James Green began using X-rays to examine fragile specimens, with George Albert Boulenger first mentioning this in a 1896 paper; their book Sciagraphs of British Batrachians and Reptiles was published in 1897. The first medical X-ray in the United States used a discharge tube designed by Ivan Puluj; Frank Austin of Dartmouth College found only Puluj’s tube produced X-rays due to its mica target. On 3 February 1896, Gilman Frost and Edwin Frost exposed Eddie McCarthy’s wrist to X-rays and captured the image on gelatin plates from Howard Langill. Many researchers, including Röntgen, developed live imaging devices using luminescent screens; Röntgen used barium platinocyanide. Enrico Salvioni and William Francis Magie developed the "cryptoscope" and "Skiascope" respectively in February 1896. Thomas Edison researched X-ray fluorescence, finding calcium tungstate was most effective, and in May 1896 developed the first mass-produced live imaging device, the "Vitascope" (later called the fluoroscope), which became standard in medical use. Edison abandoned X-ray research around 1903, before the death of Clarence Madison Dally, one of his glassblowers, who developed cancer from repeated self-exposure and had both arms amputated; he became the first known fatality from X-ray exposure in 1904. Around the same time, Mihajlo Pupin reduced exposure time from an hour to minutes by using a calcium tungstate screen developed by Edison. In 1901, U.S. President William McKinley was shot at the Pan American Exposition in Buffalo; a bullet was lodged deep in his abdomen and could not be found. A concerned aide sent for Thomas Edison to bring an X-ray machine, but it arrived and was not used; McKinley died of septic shock due to gangrene six days later. Numerous reports emerged of burns, hair loss, and other adverse effects; in February 1896, Professor John Daniel and William Lofland Dudley of Vanderbilt University reported Dudley’s bald spot (5 cm in diameter) after a one-hour exposure to X-rays. In August 1896, H. D. Hawks suffered severe burns from an X-ray demonstration, and others including Elihu Thomson, William J. Morton, and Nikola Tesla reported similar injuries; Thomson deliberately exposed a finger and suffered pain, swelling, and blistering. Some attributed damage to ultraviolet rays or ozone, while others claimed no effects. On 3 August 1905, Elizabeth Fleischman died from complications related to X-ray work. Hall-Edwards developed X-ray dermatitis, leading to amputations of his left arm at the elbow in 1908 and four fingers on his right arm soon after, leaving only a thumb; his amputated hand is preserved at Birmingham University. He died of cancer in 1926. The widespread use of X-rays led to the development of specialized Crookes tubes for generating X-rays, which were used until about 1920. A typical early 20th-century medical X-ray system used a Ruhmkorff coil connected to a cold cathode Crookes tube with a spark gap in parallel to measure voltage and determine tube "hardness" by adjusting the gap until sparks appeared. A 6.4 cm spark indicated a soft (low vacuum) tube suitable for hands and arms, 13 cm for shoulders and knees, and 18–23 cm for abdominal imaging in larger individuals. Exposure times ranged from half a minute for a hand to several minutes for a thorax, with some plates containing fluorescent salt to reduce exposure. Crookes tubes were unreliable due to gas absorption in the glass, which caused them to generate "harder" X-rays until they failed; larger tubes had "softeners" with mica that released air when heated, though the process was difficult and limited. In 1904, John Ambrose Fleming invented the thermionic diode, a hot cathode vacuum tube, which led to the development of heated-cathode X-ray tubes, known as Coolidge tubes, which replaced cold cathode tubes by about 1920. In about 1906, Charles Barkla discovered that X-rays could be scattered by gases and that each element had a characteristic X-ray spectrum, earning him the 1917 Nobel Prize in Physics. In 1912, Max von Laue, Paul Knipping, and Walter Friedrich observed X-ray diffraction by crystals, a discovery that, with work by Paul Peter Ewald, William Henry Bragg, and William Lawrence Bragg, founded X-ray crystallography. In 1913, Henry Moseley performed crystallography experiments with X-rays from metals and formulated Moseley’s law, relating X-ray frequency to atomic number. The Coolidge X-ray tube was invented in 1904 by William D. Coolidge and enabled continuous X-ray emissions; modern X-ray tubes are based on this design, often using rotating targets to dissipate heat more effectively.

X-ray tubes known as "Coolidge tubes" replaced cold cathode tubes by about 1920. In about 1906, physicist Charles Barkla discovered that X-rays could be scattered by gases and that each element has a unique X-ray spectrum, for which he received the 1917 Nobel Prize in Physics. In 1912, Max von Laue, Paul Knipping, and Walter Friedrich first observed X-ray diffraction by crystals, a discovery that, along with early work by Paul Peter Ewald, William Henry Bragg, and William Lawrence Bragg, founded X-ray crystallography. In 1913, Henry Moseley conducted crystallography experiments using X-rays from various metals and formulated Moseley's law, which links the frequency of X-rays to the atomic number of the metal. William D. Coolidge invented the Coolidge tube in 1913, enabling continuous X-ray emission; modern X-ray tubes are based on this design, often using rotating targets to improve heat dissipation and allow higher X-ray output for applications like rotational CT scanners. Major John Hall-Edwards pioneered the medical use of X-rays in Birmingham, England, and in 1908 had to amputate his left arm due to X-ray dermatitis. In 1913, Dr. Lewis Gregory Cole developed "serial radiography," a technique using motion pictures to study human physiology, such as recording a hard-boiled egg in a human stomach at one still image every four seconds in Detroit. In 1918, X-rays were combined with motion picture cameras to capture the human skeleton in motion, and in 1920, they were used to record tongue and tooth movements for language studies by the Institute of Phonetics in England. In 1914, Marie Curie developed radiological cars to support wounded soldiers in World War I, enabling rapid X-ray imaging on battlefields. From the early 1920s through the 1950s, X-ray machines were used in shoe fitting and sold to commercial shoe stores, though concerns over frequent or uncontrolled use led to decline, with Canberra proposing a ban in 1957 and Switzerland banning them in 1989. The X-ray microscope was developed in the late 1940s and early 1950s. The Chandra X-ray Observatory, launched on 23 July 1999, explores violent cosmic events such as stars torn apart by black holes, galactic collisions, novae, and neutron stars producing plasma explosions. An X-ray laser was proposed in the 1980s as part of the Reagan Administration's Strategic Defense Initiative, but a test using a thermonuclear explosion yielded inconclusive results, leading to the project's defunding—though later revived by the second Bush Administration as National Missile Defense with different technologies. Phase-contrast X-ray imaging uses phase information of X-ray beams to form images and is especially useful for soft tissue due to its sensitivity to density differences, with techniques including propagation-based phase contrast, Talbot interferometry, refraction-enhanced imaging, and X-ray interferometry. These methods offer higher contrast than standard absorption-based imaging, allowing differentiation of structures with similar densities, though they require advanced equipment such as synchrotron or microfocus sources, X-ray optics, and high-resolution detectors. X-rays with photon energies above 5–10 keV (wavelengths below 0.2–0.1 nm) are called hard X-rays; those with lower energy and longer wavelength are soft X-rays; intermediate energies are sometimes referred to as tender X-rays. Hard X-rays penetrate thick objects and are widely used in medical radiography and airport security, while soft X-rays are easily absorbed in air, with a 600 eV X-ray having an attenuation length in water less than 1 micrometer. There is no universal definition distinguishing X-rays from gamma rays; one common distinction is based on source—X-rays from electron deexcitation, gamma rays from nuclear decay—though energy ranges overlap, and classification can be ambiguous without knowing the origin. Another distinction uses wavelength, with radiation shorter than 10⁻¹¹ m (0.1 Å) classified as gamma, but this requires known wavelength. In practice, the two types often coincide, and in medical and industrial contexts, such as radiotherapy using 6–20 MeV gamma rays, the term "X-rays" may be used. X-ray photons are ionizing, capable of disrupting molecular bonds and causing harm to living tissue; high doses cause burns and radiation sickness, while lower doses increase cancer risk, though in medical imaging, the benefits generally outweigh the risks. Hard X-rays penetrate thick objects and are used in medical radiography, airport security, industrial radiography, and research like small animal CT, with penetration depth adjusted by photon energy. X-rays have much shorter wavelengths than visible light, enabling imaging of structures smaller than those visible under a microscope, used in X-ray microscopy and crystallography. X-rays interact with matter through photoabsorption, Compton scattering, and Rayleigh scattering; the strength depends on photon energy and elemental composition, not chemical properties. Photoabsorption dominates in soft X-rays and low-energy hard X-rays, with the probability proportional to Z³/E³ (where Z is atomic number and E is photon energy), though absorption edges cause abrupt changes near inner shell binding energies. For soft tissue, photoabsorption dominates up to about 26 keV, after which Compton scattering takes over; calcium (Z=20) in bones gives them high contrast in radiographs due to high atomic number and density. A photoabsorbed photon transfers all its energy to an electron, ionizing the atom and producing a photoelectron that may ionize further atoms; when an outer electron fills a vacancy, a characteristic X-ray or Auger electron is emitted, enabling elemental detection via X-ray or Auger electron spectroscopy. Compton scattering is the dominant interaction in soft tissue in medical imaging, involving inelastic scattering of X-rays by outer shell electrons, with part of the photon's energy transferred to the electron, increasing the photon's wavelength; the scattered photon can go in any direction, with higher probability near the original direction, and the transferred energy can be calculated from the scattering angle using energy and momentum conservation. Rayleigh scattering is the dominant elastic scattering mechanism in the X-ray regime, producing a refractive index slightly below 1. X-rays are produced when charged particles (electrons or ions) of sufficient energy strike a material. In an X-ray tube, a high voltage accelerates electrons from a hot cathode to a metal anode, where they collide and generate X-rays. In medical tubes, tungsten or a rhenium-tungsten alloy (5% and 95%) is commonly used, with molybdenum for mammography; in crystallography, copper is common, cobalt when iron fluorescence is a concern, and aluminum or magnesium for low-energy applications like X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. The maximum X-ray photon energy equals the tube voltage times the electron charge, so an 80 kV tube cannot produce X-rays above 80 keV. The output consists of a continuous Bremsstrahlung spectrum falling to zero at the tube voltage plus characteristic spikes. Diagnostic tubes operate between 20 kV and 150 kV, producing X-rays from 20 keV to 150 keV. Both Bremsstrahlung and characteristic X-ray production are inefficient, with only about 1% of electrical energy converted to X-rays, and the rest released as waste heat, requiring careful heat dissipation design. Synchrotron radiation, generated by particle accelerators, is increasingly used in research due to its high intensity, broad spectrum, excellent collimation, and linear polarization. Short nanosecond bursts of X-rays peaking at 15 keV can be produced by peeling pressure-sensitive tape in a moderate vacuum, likely due to triboelectric charging, and are sufficient for X-ray imaging. Fast protons or positive ions also produce X-rays, used in analytical procedures like particle-induced X-ray emission, with cross sections proportional to Z₁¹²Z₂⁻⁴ (Z₁ = ion atomic number, Z₂ = target atomic number). X-rays are produced in lightning during terrestrial gamma-ray flashes via electron acceleration and Bremsstrahlung, generating photons from a few keV to tens of MeV; in lab discharges with a 1-meter gap and 1 MV peak voltage, 160 keV X-rays are observed, possibly due to streamer interactions or air perturbations facilitating runaway electrons. X-ray detectors vary by function; imaging detectors like those in radiography were originally photographic plates or film but are now mostly digital, such as image plates or flat panel detectors; ionization chambers assess direct exposure hazards, dosimeters measure radiation dose, and X-ray spectra are measured via energy or wavelength dispersive spectrometers; hybrid photon counting detectors are common in X-ray diffraction. Since Röntgen's discovery that X-rays can reveal bone structures, they have been used in medical imaging; the first medical use occurred less than a month after his paper, and by 2010, five billion medical imaging examinations had been conducted worldwide, with medical imaging radiation exposure accounting for about 50% of total ionizing radiation exposure in the U.S. in 2006. Projectional radiography produces two-dimensional images using X-rays; bones, rich in calcium (high atomic number), absorb X-rays efficiently, reducing transmission and making them visible; lungs and gas-filled areas show up due to lower absorption, while tissue differences are harder to detect. These images are useful for detecting skeletal pathologies and some soft tissue diseases, such as pneumonia, lung cancer, pulmonary edema, bowel obstruction, free air, and free fluid in ascites; gallstones and kidney stones may also be detected. Projectional radiographs are less effective for imaging soft tissues like the brain or muscle, but are widely used to evaluate orthopedic implants such as knee, hip, or shoulder replacements in two dimensions or three dimensions via "2D to 3D registration" to reduce projection errors. Dental radiography is commonly used to diagnose cavities. In medical diagnostics, low-energy (soft) X-rays are undesirable because they are fully absorbed by the body, increasing radiation dose without contributing to the image; thus, a thin aluminum filter is placed over the X-ray tube window to absorb these low-energy components.

X-rays are used to detect various pathologies, such as gallstones (which are rarely radiopaque) or kidney stones (which are often, but not always, visible), and may be employed in diagnosing conditions like ascites. Traditional plain X-rays are less effective for imaging soft tissues such as the brain or muscle, but are widely used to evaluate the position of orthopedic implants like knee, hip, or shoulder replacements in relation to surrounding bone—this can be assessed in two dimensions from plain radiographs or in three dimensions using a technique called '2D to 3D registration,' which is said to eliminate projection errors. Dental radiography is commonly used to diagnose oral issues such as cavities. In medical imaging, low-energy (soft) X-rays are undesirable because they are completely absorbed by the body, increasing radiation dose without contributing to the image; thus, a thin aluminium filter is placed over the X-ray tube to absorb these low-energy rays, hardening the beam by shifting the spectrum toward higher-energy (harder) X-rays. For cardiovascular imaging via angiography, an initial image is taken of a region of interest, followed by a second image after injecting an iodinated contrast agent into the blood vessels; the two images are digitally subtracted to reveal only the contrast outlining the vessels, which is then compared to normal anatomical images to detect vessel damage or blockages. Computed tomography (CT scanning) produces cross-sectional images from a series of two-dimensional X-ray images taken in different directions, which can be combined into a three-dimensional body image; CT scans are faster and more cost-effective than other methods and are used for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. Fluoroscopy provides real-time moving images of internal structures using a fluoroscope, which may include a contrast agent and is used in procedures such as cardiac catheterization, embolization, and barium swallow; modern fluoroscopy uses short bursts of X-rays instead of continuous beams to reduce radiation exposure. X-rays are also used in radiation therapy for cancer management, including palliation, with lower-energy beams used for skin cancers and higher-energy beams for internal cancers such as brain, lung, prostate, and breast. X-rays are classified as carcinogens by the World Health Organization's International Agency for Research on Cancer and the U.S. government, and diagnostic X-rays—especially CT scans—increase the risk of cancer and developmental problems; it is estimated that 0.4% of current U.S. cancers are due to past CT scans, with this potentially rising to 1.5–2% at 2007 usage rates. There is no established threshold dose below which cancer risk is zero, though this is increasingly questioned; cancer risk begins at 1100 mGy, and diagnostic X-rays are estimated to increase the average person’s lifetime cancer risk by 0.6–3.0% by age 75. Radiation exposure varies by test and body part; a plain chest X-ray equals about 10 days of background radiation, while a dental X-ray equals one day; each adds less than 1 in 1,000,000 to lifetime cancer risk. An abdominal or chest CT equals 2–3 years of background radiation (or 4–5 years for abdomen/chest), increasing lifetime cancer risk from 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 10,000, compared to a 40% lifetime cancer risk in the U.S. A chest CT has an effective dose of about 5 mSv and absorbed dose of 14 mGy, while a head CT (1.5 mSv, 64 mGy) performed twice—once with and once without contrast—equals 40 years of background radiation to the head; effective dose estimation has a uncertainty range of ±19% to ±32% for adult head scans. Radiation poses greater risk to fetuses, so in pregnant patients, the benefits of X-rays must be weighed against potential harm to the fetus; one scan in nine months may be harmful, and therefore ultrasounds are preferred in pregnancy as they do not use radiation. Excessive radiation exposure can harm the fetus or maternal reproductive organs. In the U.S., there are approximately 62 million CT scans annually, including over 4 million in children. Avoiding unnecessary X-rays, especially CT scans, reduces radiation dose and associated cancer risk. Medical X-rays were responsible for 58% of human-made radiation exposure in the U.S. in 1987, accounting for 10% of total radiation exposure (out of 18% from human-made sources, with 82% from natural sources), and by 2006, medical procedures contributed nearly half of all radiation exposure due to increased use of imaging, particularly CT scans and nuclear medicine. Dental X-ray exposure ranges from 5 to 40 μSv per procedure (depending on type and technology), with a full mouth series ranging from 60 (digital) to 180 (film) μSv, and an annual average of up to 400 μSv. Financial incentives have been shown to increase X-ray usage, as doctors paid a separate fee per X-ray perform more. Early photon tomography (EPT), as of 2015, and other techniques are being researched as potential alternatives to X-rays. Although X-rays are outside the visible spectrum, under special conditions they can be faintly seen by the dark-adapted human eye, as reported by Brandes and Röntgen, who observed a blue-gray glow within the eye or from a tube behind a wooden door; this effect is likely due to Cherenkov radiation or direct retinal excitation, though the exact mechanism remains unclear. At very high intensities, X-ray beams can ionize air molecules and produce visible effects, such as at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility’s wiggler beamline. The ionizing ability of X-rays is measured as exposure, while the energy absorbed by matter is measured as absorbed dose; the equivalent dose, which reflects biological impact on human tissue, equals the absorbed dose for X-rays.
